ego.name: Geoffrey Bawa
ego.summary: Geoffrey Bawa was a Sri Lankan architect and a leading figure in Tropical Modernism. His work combined modern construction with Sri Lankan climatic conditions, landscapes, courtyards, water, local materials, and artistic craftsmanship.

connections.relationship_description: Geoffrey Bawa’s father was a Sri Lankan lawyer. Bawa first pursued legal education before leaving the profession for architecture.
connections.notes: Benjamin Bawa died in 1923, when Geoffrey was a child.

connections.relationship_description: Geoffrey Bawa’s mother was of mixed Sinhalese, German, and Scottish descent. Her death in 1946 preceded his departure from legal practice and two years of travel abroad.
connections.notes: She was of mixed Sinhalese, German, and Scottish descent.

connections.relationship_description: Bevis Bawa was Geoffrey Bawa’s older brother and became a landscape architect in Sri Lanka.
connections.notes: The brothers were both gay and moved within overlapping artistic and social networks.

connections.relationship_description: H. H. Reid apprenticed Geoffrey Bawa at the Colombo architectural practice Edwards, Reid and Begg in 1951. Reid’s death led Bawa to seek formal architectural education in England.
connections.notes: After Reid's death in 1952, Bawa returned to England for formal architectural education and later took over what remained of Reid's practice.

connections.relationship_description: Danish architect Ulrik Plesner joined Bawa’s Colombo practice as a partner in 1959. They designed many buildings together before Plesner left Sri Lanka in 1967.
connections.notes: Their joint work included Ekala Industrial Estate, Good Shepherd Chapel, Polontolawa House, and St. Thomas Preparatory School.

connections.relationship_description: De Silva began a long-term professional relationship with Bawa after he designed her Colombo house in 1960, creating batik tapestries for buildings including Bentota Beach Hotel and the Sri Lankan Parliament Building.
connections.notes: Their collaboration connected Bawa's architecture to the revival of Sri Lankan batik and craft traditions.

connections.relationship_description: Sansoni was a close friend and design collaborator who produced murals, textiles, and furnishings for several Bawa projects, including the Bentota Beach Hotel, Kandalama Hotel, and Lighthouse Hotel.
connections.notes: She also coauthored a 1996 publication on Bawa with him and Brian Brace Taylor.

connections.relationship_description: Senanayake worked first as a draughtsman in Bawa's office and later contributed commissioned sculpture and decorative work to Bawa projects, including the Bentota Beach Hotel and Parliament building.
connections.notes: His bird-inspired metal sculptures and other artworks became integral features of several Bawa interiors.

connections.relationship_description: As president of Sri Lanka, Jayewardene invited Bawa in 1979 to design the new Sri Lankan Parliament building at Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte, completed in 1982.
connections.notes: The commission became one of Bawa's most prominent public projects.

connections.relationship_description: Friend was part of Bawa's wide circle of friendships among gay artists working across Sri Lanka and Oceania.
connections.notes: Friend spent substantial periods in Ceylon during the late 1950s and early 1960s.

connections.relationship_description: Paynter belonged to Bawa's circle of gay artist friends in Sri Lanka.
connections.notes: Paynter was a major Sri Lankan painter known especially for murals and portraiture.

connections.relationship_description: Wendt was included among the gay artists in Bawa's wider friendship circle in Sri Lanka.
connections.notes: Wendt died in 1944, before Bawa's architectural career began.

category_summaries.summary: Bawa’s family connected him to law and landscape. His father was a Sri Lankan lawyer, and Bawa first studied law in England. His mother’s death in 1946 preceded his departure from legal practice. His older brother Bevis became a landscape architect in Sri Lanka.

Bawa entered architecture through an apprenticeship with H. H. Reid in Colombo. Reid’s death in 1952 led Bawa back to England for formal study. Bawa returned to Sri Lanka in 1957 and took over Reid’s remaining practice. His partnership with Ulrik Plesner began in 1959, and President J. R. Jayewardene invited him to design the new Parliament building in 1979.

Bawa worked with artists and designers including Ena de Silva, Barbara Sansoni, and Laki Senanayake. Their association brought textiles, batik, sculpture, murals, and furniture into architectural projects in Sri Lanka. The group’s work contributed to a renewed awareness of indigenous materials and crafts after independence.

Bawa’s friendships with gay artists connected him to Sri Lanka’s modern arts community and to artists working across Oceania. The circle included David Paynter, Lionel Wendt, and Donald Friend. The available record identifies friendships rather than specific joint projects.
